trades.headline: Flip a hot committee back and a WR3 for Baltimore's No. 1 before his price recovers
trades.summary: Jonah Coleman's recent spike looks role-dependent and unsustainable; Zay Flowers still owns Baltimore's passing game despite a 30-day price dip.

give: Coleman is running 54% over his own projection (11.3 vs 7.3 ppg) on just 50% snaps and a 10% target share - that gap closes fast once touchdowns regress.
Harvey and Dobbins are both still active in Denver's backfield behind him, so this isn't a clean workhorse takeover yet.
Lemon is a fringe FLEX piece (6.1 ppg, 19% target share) you won't miss in your lineup.
get: Flowers is still drawing a 28% target share and 7.9 targets per game for Baltimore - the WR1 job hasn't moved even as his price slid 11% over 30 days.
Higbee adds a 64%-snap, 12%-target-share TE for almost nothing, a free bye-week option behind Tyler Warren.
you: Flowers starts immediately at WR, your thinnest position; Monangai slides into the vacated FLEX spot so you don't lose a roster slot.
them: Njgriffin is 0-10 and thin at both RB and WR - Coleman (a rookie who just took over snaps in Denver) and Lemon (a rookie already playing 79% of Philadelphia's snaps) are exactly the long-term youth a rebuilding team should want over an established 26-year-old WR.
experts: Rotowire's offseason breakdown still frames Flowers as Baltimore's clear top target with little depth behind him in the passing game.

DraftSharks and FantasyNerds both describe Coleman as having 'reclaimed' Denver's lead role only because Harvey and Dobbins are compromised - the kind of overheated storyline a sell should get ahead of.

risks: If Harvey and Dobbins both land on IR and Coleman becomes a true every-down back, this looks like a bad sell in hindsight.
Flowers' price keeps sliding if Lamar Jackson's ankle lingers and caps Baltimore's passing volume.

trades.headline: Sell two banged-up committee backs to an 8-2 contender, buy Henry and Barkley near their floor
trades.summary: Henry's dip traces to Lamar Jackson's injury and Baltimore's offense, not his own decline; Barkley's an efficient back buried by Philadelphia's erratic usage, not a talent drop.

give: Coleman is outscoring his projection by 54% on a 10% target share - his trade value is as high as it will get before that TD rate normalizes.

Monangai is currently Out with a recurring knee injury after already missing the Week 5-9 stretch; his gaudy 15.7 ppg is from before this latest setback, so the name still carries that stat line for now.
get: Henry is within a point of his own projection (15.3 vs 15.8 ppg) and still getting a 20.2-touch, 4.3-red-zone-look workhorse role - his price is down 36% in 30 days purely because Baltimore's offense has struggled since Lamar Jackson got hurt, and the team has told reporters he isn't being traded.
Barkley is averaging 5.7 yards per carry when actually used; the drop in his price (-12% in 30 days) reflects Philadelphia's inconsistent usage in a lost season, not a loss of ability.
you: Henry starts immediately at RB and Barkley slides into your FLEX, pushing Coleman and Charbonnet to the bench - an upgrade at both spots.
them: stplohasz is 8-2 but still tagged thin at RB; both of their backs carry wear-and-tear questions this year, so shipping them out for a rookie who just inherited touches in Denver (Coleman) and a cheap buy-low flier (Monangai) fits a contender hedging its oldest, most banged-up RB room.
experts: ESPN's Adam Schefter and multiple outlets report Baltimore has told teams Henry isn't going anywhere at the deadline, and that his drop-off traces to the offense struggling around Lamar Jackson's injury, not Henry himself.
ClutchPoints' breakdown of Philadelphia's handling of Barkley calls it 'bizarre and wrong,' arguing the fix is changing his usage, not that he's lost his juice.

risks: Barkley is also dealing with a hamstring/back issue, and the Eagles have given no sign they'll feed him more volume soon - if Philadelphia stays pass-heavy in losses, this doesn't pay off right away.
Monangai's knee is unresolved; if he's out deep into December, you're selling an asset that's already near its bottom, not its peak.

trades.headline: Buy Philadelphia's WR1 while he's hurt, add a TE1 who just got paid
trades.summary: DeVonta Smith's per-target production is elite when he plays; Brenton Strange just signed a three-year extension and is Jacksonville's clear TE1.

give: Lemon is a complementary WR3 (19% target share) on your roster - easy to spend.
A 2027 2nd you won't use this season is the right currency for a win-now WR/TE upgrade.
get: Smith is drawing a 33% target share and 86% snaps when active and outscoring his projection (1.18x) - he hasn't lost the job, he's hurt, and that's why his price is down 14% over 30 days.
Strange posted a 26.2% target share over his last two games and just signed a three-year, $48M extension that locks him in as Jacksonville's TE1.
you: Smith starts at WR as soon as he's active, directly addressing your thinnest position; Strange is a real TE2 behind Tyler Warren. You can drop Odell Beckham Jr. to make the roster spot.
them: Purple Cobras are 3-7 and thin at TE/QB but deep at WR - moving a hurt receiver they're already stocked at for a future pick plus a complementary WR (Lemon) fits a team pointed at next year.
experts: Smith has been dealing with a recurring hamstring since Week 4, was ruled out again in Week 9, and still wasn't practicing as of Nov. 10 - an extended absence, not a lost role, is why the price is down.
Jacksonville's own announcement of Strange's extension, plus head coach Liam Coen's comments about wanting to get him 'out in space more,' signal the team is building its passing game around him.

risks: Smith's return timeline is still unconfirmed as of this week - if the hamstring drags into December, his price could keep sliding before it recovers. Check Friday's injury report before pulling the trigger.
Strange still splits targets with Brian Thomas Jr. and Jakobi Meyers, so his ceiling is capped versus a true WR1-type tight end.

trades.headline: Trade down from an early 2027 1st - this league's own draft history says it's overpriced
trades.summary: Early first-round rookie picks in this league have historically returned far less than market price; add a hot rookie WR and still bank the gap.

give: An early 2027 1st doesn't help your 2026 playoff push, and it's the exact slot this league's own draft history says the market overpays for.
get: This league's last 20 first-round rookie picks turned into a median value of 2,609; early-slot picks specifically landed at 3,633 - well under the 5,117 the market is charging for an early 1st today.
Trading down to a mid 1st (market price 3,370, much closer to what early picks actually turn into) plus Denzel Boston, a rookie playing a 90% snap share, banks that gap right now.
you: Boston slots into your FLEX, and you still hold a future 1st (now via paparik69, mid slot) for next year's class.
them: Purple Cobras are rebuilding at 3-7 and already deep at WR - they'd rather bet on an unproven early slot two years out than keep a player who's already outscoring his rookie-WR projection.
experts: Boston had 20 catches for 372 yards and 3 touchdowns through his first seven games, starting alongside Jerry Jeudy and KC Concepcion - a strong floor for a rookie, matching the pre-draft scouting that tagged him a day-one outside starter.

risks: Boston was questionable with a toe injury in Week 10, though he returned to practice as a limited participant and was trending toward playing - worth a Friday injury-report check, but not a role change.
If Boston's target share shrinks as Cleveland's receiver room gets healthier, this looks like you overpaid for a hot month.
A 2027 mid 1st is still just a projection two years out - this league's history shows 0% of its last 20 first-rounders busted, but that's no guarantee going forward.

trades.headline: Cash out two fast-depreciating backs for Arizona's new starting QB and a Vikings backup with contingent value
trades.summary: Monangai and Kiner both have short half-lives; Carson Beck just became Arizona's starter after Gardner Minshew's season-ending injury, and Jordan Mason is a Jones setback away from a bigger role.

give: Kiner's 30-day value is up 480% purely because he filled in for an injured starter - that kind of spike corrects itself fast once the starter's healthy.
Monangai is currently Out with a recurring knee injury; his season-long per-game numbers are inflated by games before this setback.
get: Beck is Arizona's starting QB as of Week 11, not a backup - Gardner Minshew's season-ending elbow injury handed him the job outright, and he's still priced like a third-stringer.

Mason is buried in single-digit touches behind a 31-year-old Aaron Jones right now, but that's exactly why he's cheap - a Jones setback or decline hands Mason back the early-down work he had before Jones returned.
you: This is a depth-for-depth swap that doesn't change your Week 11 lineup, but it converts two bench pieces at their peak name value into younger, more controllable assets.
them: THE CREAM TEAM is thin at RB and deep at QB - shedding a backup QB (Beck) and a blocked RB (Mason) for two bodies at their thin position is a straightforward volume upgrade for them.
experts: Local Arizona outlets note Beck was a third-string QB just 11 days before his first start, named starter against the Rams after Minshew went on IR - a fast-tracked opportunity the market hasn't caught up to yet.
CBS Sports' game logs show Mason getting single-digit touches to Jones' high-teens workload in recent games - a real role gap, but one that flips fast if Jones (31) misses time.

risks: Neither piece helps your lineup today - this only pays off if Beck keeps the job past this year or Jones' workload opens up for Mason.
If Beck struggles as a first-time starter behind a banged-up offensive line, or Jones stays entrenched, both pieces stall out as bench clutter.
